title: Set up Xcode on a new Mac
tagline: From a blank machine to a build on TestFlight, for anyone already paying for the Apple Developer Program.
intro: You have paid the 99 USD and you are holding a Mac with nothing on it. This is the short path to a setup that builds and ships.
Work through the sections in order — each one assumes the one above it is done.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: Five stages. Everything below fits into one of them.

blocks.caption: The whole route, blank machine to TestFlight.

items.label: Prepare
items.detail: Sign in, free up about 60 GB, and update macOS first — Xcode refuses an older one
explain: Xcode is about 20 GB on its own, and simulator runtimes, device support files and derived data pile up on top — 60 GB free is where the install stops failing half way through.
Every Xcode names the oldest macOS it will run on and refuses to install below it, so updating the OS first saves downloading those 20 GB twice.

items.label: Install Xcode
items.detail: App Store for the latest; a .xip or the xcodes CLI when you need one exact version
explain: The App Store only ever offers the newest Xcode, which is what you want unless a project pins an older toolchain or a CI image you have to match.
A .xip from Apple's developer downloads, or the xcodes CLI, gets you one exact version — and several versions can sit side by side in /Applications.
However it arrives, open it once by hand: the first launch installs the extra components, and nothing built from the terminal works until it has.

items.label: Toolchain
items.detail: Point xcode-select at Xcode, accept the licence, then install Homebrew and the project tools
explain: xcode-select points every command line tool at one Xcode. With two versions installed, it is the switch that decides which one xcodebuild and swift actually use.
The licence is accepted once per Xcode, and a CI build that fails with nothing but a licence message is almost always this step.
Homebrew then carries the rest — CocoaPods, fastlane, whatever the project's README asks for — so the toolchain is reproducible instead of remembered.

items.label: Signing
items.detail: Add your Apple ID so Xcode can issue a certificate and fetch the profile a device needs
explain: Adding the Apple ID under Settings → Accounts lets Xcode issue a development certificate and drop its private key straight into this Mac's Keychain.
Automatic signing then fetches, and re-fetches, the provisioning profile whenever the bundle id, the capabilities or the list of devices changes.

items.label: Ship
items.detail: Run on a real iPhone to prove signing works, then archive and upload to TestFlight
explain: A run on a real iPhone is the proof that signing works: the simulator never checks a certificate, so it happily runs an app that could not be installed anywhere.
Archive builds the Release configuration and hands it to the Organizer, which is where the upload to App Store Connect and TestFlight starts.

items: Sign in to your Apple Account in System Settings
Install Xcode, Command Line Tools and a simulator runtime
Accept the Xcode license
Install Homebrew and the project's tooling
Add your Apple ID under Xcode → Settings → Accounts
Let Xcode issue a Development certificate
Register test device UDIDs if you sign manually
Create an App Store Connect API key for CI
Run on a real device, then archive to TestFlight

sections.title: Prepare the machine
sections.summary: Three things to get right before you start downloading.

items: Disk — Xcode is about 15 GB and each simulator runtime another 7 – 10 GB. Keep 60 GB free.
Apple Account — sign in with the Apple ID that owns the Developer Program. Two-factor is mandatory on it.
macOS version — every Xcode has a minimum. Update macOS first; the other order fails halfway.

sections.title: Signing
sections.summary: The part that goes wrong. Nothing carries over with your Apple ID — this machine needs its own certificate.

rows: Your identity with Apple, useless without its private key.
The bundle id plus the capabilities it may use.
Apple's signed statement tying the two to a list of devices.

blocks.caption: Three inputs, one profile, one signed app.

items.label: Certificate
items.detail: Your identity with Apple. Useless without the private key, which lives only in this Mac's Keychain
explain: The certificate is the public half; the private key beside it in the Keychain is what actually signs. Apple keeps no copy, so a lost key cannot be downloaded again.
Moving to another Mac means exporting both halves as a .p12 — or revoking the certificate and issuing a new one, which invalidates what the old one signed.
A development certificate signs builds for registered devices; a distribution certificate signs what goes to TestFlight and the store.

items.label: App ID
items.detail: The bundle id plus the capabilities the app may use, such as push or App Groups
explain: The bundle id has to match the project character for character. A wildcard App ID exists, but it cannot carry push, App Groups or anything else that needs an entitlement.
Turning a capability on in Xcode edits the App ID at Apple's end too, which is why the profile has to be re-issued immediately after.

items.label: Devices
items.detail: UDIDs of the phones allowed to run the build. Not needed once the app ships through the store
explain: A development profile lists the UDIDs it covers, so a phone registered after the profile was issued needs that profile downloading again.
The account has a device limit per year, and removing a device only frees the slot when the membership renews.

items.label: Provisioning profile
items.detail: Apple's signed statement tying those three together. Xcode downloads it and embeds it in the app
explain: It is a signed file holding your certificate, the App ID with its entitlements, and the device list — sealed by Apple so the phone can check the app is allowed to run.
It ships inside the .app as embedded.mobileprovision, and it expires — a year for development — which is why an old build stops launching one day for no visible reason.

items.label: Signed app
items.detail: Runs on the registered devices, and is the only form App Store Connect will accept
explain: iOS checks the signature at install and at every launch: every entitlement in the binary has to be covered by the profile, or the app is refused.
App Store Connect rejects an unsigned or wrongly signed upload before processing even starts, which is the error most pipelines meet first.

items: Target → Signing & Capabilities → tick Automatically manage signing.
Pick your team; Xcode creates the certificate, the App ID and the profile.
Use this unless something forces you not to.

body: You get 2 Development and 3 Distribution certificates per account. When Xcode says the limit is reached, revoke an old one in the portal — do not create a second account.

blocks.text: Manual signing, for teams and CI

items: Create a CSR: Keychain Access → Certificate Assistant → Request a Certificate from a Certificate Authority, saved to disk.
Portal → Certificates → upload the CSR, download the .cer and double-click it.
Portal → Identifiers → create the App ID and enable the capabilities the app uses.
Portal → Devices → add the UDIDs, then Profiles → create and download the profile.
fastlane match does all of the above once, for the whole team.
It keeps the certificates and profiles encrypted in a git repo.
The next machine needs only read access and the passphrase.

sections.title: App Store Connect
sections.summary: Create the app record, then the key that lets CI upload without a 2FA prompt.

items: My Apps → New App.
Fill in platform, app name and primary language.
Pick a bundle id created in the portal beforehand, and an SKU of your own.
Users and Access → Integrations → App Store Connect API → add a key.
App Manager is enough; Admin only if it must manage users.
Download the .p8 and note the Key ID and Issuer ID.

blocks.caption: Those three values are the whole login for CI.

items.label: .p8 key file
items.detail: The private key file. It downloads exactly once — lose it and the only fix is a new key
explain: Keep it in the CI secret store, never in the repository: anyone holding the file and the two ids can upload builds as your team.
Apple offers the download exactly once. If it is lost, revoke that key and create another — nothing brings the file itself back.

items.label: Key ID
items.detail: Short id shown beside the key, telling Apple which of your keys is signing
explain: It is not a secret, only a name: it travels in the token header so Apple knows which public key to check the signature against.
Keys are revoked one at a time, so giving CI its own key keeps a colleague's laptop out of the blast radius.

items.label: Issuer ID
items.detail: Identifies your team. The same value for every key the account creates
explain: Read it once from the top of the Keys page in App Store Connect; every key the team ever creates carries the same one.
It names the team the token speaks for, which starts to matter the moment your Apple ID belongs to more than one.

items.label: fastlane / altool
items.detail: Signs a short-lived token from those three values, so nobody has to type a 2FA code
explain: The three values become a short-lived JWT, signed locally. It expires in minutes, so a leaked token is worth far less than the key that made it.
This is the whole reason a pipeline can upload at three in the morning: no password, no 2FA prompt, nothing waiting on a human with a phone.

items.label: TestFlight
items.detail: The build lands here and can go to testers, with nothing interactive in the pipeline
explain: Processing takes a few minutes after the upload, and a build is only installable once it finishes and the export compliance question is answered.
Internal testers get the build straight away; an external group waits for a review, so leave a day for the first one.

body: The .p8 downloads exactly once. Lose it and the only fix is a new key.

items: Push notifications need a second key from the same page: APNs.
One APNs .p8 covers development, production and every app in the team.

sections.title: First build
sections.summary: Get through these three and the setup is proven.

items: Run on a simulator — proves the toolchain and the runtime.
Run on a real iPhone, with Developer Mode enabled under Settings → Privacy & Security — proves signing.
Product → Archive → Distribute App → TestFlight & App Store — proves distribution.

sections.title: Common errors
sections.summary: Four messages cover most of the time lost here.

rows: The machine has no private key yet. Xcode → Settings → Accounts → Manage Certificates → add one.
The profile predates the certificate. Edit it in the portal, tick the certificate, save, then download profiles again.
The UDID is not in the profile. Add the device and regenerate, or switch to automatic signing.
xcode-select points at the Command Line Tools instead of Xcode.app. Point it back.

sections.summary: Do this today and the next machine takes an afternoon.

items: Both certificates exported as .p12, with their passwords
The App Store Connect .p8 and the APNs .p8
Key ID, Issuer ID and Team ID
Your bundle ids and the capabilities each one enables

body: Keep them in a password manager, never in the repo. Without the .p12 a private key cannot be recovered, only replaced.
